idea: A wearable device for continuous glucose monitoring using non-invasive optical sensors, sold to people with type 2 diabetes who dislike finger-prick tests.

market.finding: The non-invasive blood glucose monitoring system market was valued at USD 34 million in 2024 and is projected to reach USD 316.65 million by 2034 (25% CAGR).
The continuous glucose monitoring market was valued at USD 12.4 billion in 2025 and is expected to reach USD 55.5 billion in 2035, a 16.3% CAGR from 2026 to 2035.
The FDA has never authorized a noninvasive wearable that measures blood glucose on its own, and Verily stopped its glucose-sensing contact lens in 2018 after tests showed insufficient consistency.
Whoop has filed a patent, reported in 2026, for a non-invasive method of measuring blood sugar in a wearable.
Afon Technology describes its Glucowear as the world's first non-invasive, real-time continuous glucose monitor; this is the company's own claim and the source gives no year or figures.

brief.summary: Non-invasive glucose monitoring is a small but fast-growing niche inside a large CGM market, valued at USD 34 million in 2024 and projected to reach USD 316.65 million by 2034 (E14, E15). The main patent risk is that several optical glucose patents may still be in force, including reflectometry (E8), a non-invasive glucose device (E11) and wearable optical pathways (E12). Large players are also filing new patents (E17).
brief.white_space: The records do not seem to show an FDA-authorized standalone non-invasive glucose wearable (E16), and none appear to target a comfort-first product for type 2 users who mainly want fewer finger pricks. This is a rough read and needs attorney review.

pathways.name: Build on expired near-infrared and self-calibration art
pathways.detail: Several older patents on compact NIR glucose measurement, portable non-invasive monitors and self-calibrating sensors appear to be past their term. They may be useful as a technical starting point. Have counsel confirm their status and check for later continuations.

pathways.name: Design around live optical patents
pathways.detail: Map the claims of the patents that may still be in force on reflectometry, non-invasive glucose devices and wearable optical pathways. Then choose a sensing method and housing that steer clear of their specific claim elements.

pathways.name: Partner or license as an adjunct to existing CGMs
pathways.detail: No standalone non-invasive device has FDA authorization. One option is to position the wearable as a trend or wellness companion, or to partner with a CGM incumbent for calibration and regulatory paths. Expired CGM receiver and delivery patents may also inform how the system is integrated.

assumption_to_test.assumption: Type 2 users who dislike finger pricks would pay for, and trust, a non-invasive wearable that gives approximate trend readings rather than exact clinical values.
assumption_to_test.how_to_test: Run a $300 targeted ad campaign to type 2 diabetes communities. Point it to a landing page describing a trend-only, no-needle wearable with a price and a refundable $1 reservation. Add 10 short follow-up interviews over two weeks. Measure the reservation rate and how much accuracy users say they need.

attorney_questions: Do the claims of US10779755B2, US8235897B2 or US20150099943A1 appear to read on a wrist-worn optical glucose wearable, and are these patents actually still in force (E8, E11, E12)?
Are there live continuations or related patents tied to the expired NIR and self-calibration patents (E5, E9, E10) that could still matter?
Should we monitor or oppose Whoop's reported non-invasive glucose filing, and does it narrow our options for claiming our own method (E17)?
